Garissa Insecurity: Research + Computational Extension

Ziebi Kofa Maro · BA Political Science, The Catholic University of Eastern Africa

This notebook is the computational companion to my undergraduate thesis, Assessment of Kenya's Current Insecurity Challenges: A Case Study of Security Challenges in Garissa County (2023). The full thesis — original fieldwork, 397 survey responses, 20 key-informant interviews, 4 focus group discussions, documented sampling methodology, and qualitative thematic analysis — lives alongside this notebook at layer-a-original-research/Garissa_Insecurity_Thesis_Portfolio.docx. That document is the real research. This notebook does not repeat it — it extends it with a reproducible quantitative layer.

What's in this notebook

Part Basis What it shows
Part 1 — Descriptive reproduction Real, reported thesis figures Rebuilding a real research finding as a reproducible, testable artifact
Part 2 — ML pipeline demonstration Synthetic data, built to match the real margins Building, evaluating, and interpreting a standard supervised-learning pipeline end to end

Why synthetic data in Part 2: respondent-level data from the original 2023 fieldwork was not retained — only the aggregate tables in Chapter Four survive. Part 2's target variable and two supporting fields are generated to match those real aggregate margins, then given an illustrative correlation structure so a classification pipeline has something non-trivial to recover. Model results in Part 2 are not evidence about Garissa County — they demonstrate that the pipeline is built and evaluated correctly. This is stated at every relevant point below, not just here.

A curated list of real, public datasets (ACLED, UNHCR, KNBS, GTD) that could replace Part 2 with genuine findings in a follow-up study is at layer-b-computational-extension/data/external_datasets.md.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
import os

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10,
                      "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

NAVY, RUST, SAND, SAGE = "#1f3a5f", "#c0562b", "#d9a441", "#5b7f5e"
PALETTE = [NAVY, RUST, SAND, SAGE, "#7a6fa6", "#3f8f8a", "#a54848", "#5a5a5a"]
RNG = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
RANDOM_STATE = 42

print("Environment ready.")
Environment ready.

Part 1 — Descriptive Reproduction (Real Data)

Tables 4.1–4.4 and Figures 4.1–4.5 in the thesis report real, aggregated descriptive statistics from the actual 397-respondent survey. The cells below reconstruct a respondent-level table from those real reported margins — gender × age category (Table 4.3) — and a sub-county allocation consistent with the quota-sampling design, then rebuild every Chapter Four figure and the chi-square test from that reconstruction.

# Gender x Age category -- reproduces Table 4.3 exactly (n = 397), using the
# counts as originally captioned (Male n=234, Female n=163). See the
# data-quality note below on why these labels, not the Fig 4.1 percentages,
# are used as the basis for reconstruction.
age_gender_counts = {
    ("Male", "18-35"): 20, ("Male", "36-50"): 137, ("Male", "51-65"): 40, ("Male", "Above 65"): 37,
    ("Female", "18-35"): 21, ("Female", "36-50"): 92, ("Female", "51-65"): 46, ("Female", "Above 65"): 4,
}
assert sum(age_gender_counts.values()) == 397

rows = []
rid = 1
for (gender, age_cat), n in age_gender_counts.items():
    for _ in range(n):
        rows.append({"respondent_id": rid, "gender": gender, "age_category": age_cat})
        rid += 1
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# Sub-county: Table 4.4 in the original document reports counts that sum to
# 496, not the stated n=397 (100 + 99*4 = 496) -- a transcription error
# inherited from the 2023 submission. We allocate as evenly as possible
# across the five sub-counties instead, consistent with the quota-sampling
# target of an equal ~20% share described in the thesis's methodology.
subcounties = ["Fafi", "Garissa", "Lagdera", "Dadaab", "Balambala"]
base, remainder = divmod(397, 5)
counts = [base + 1 if i < remainder else base for i in range(5)]
RNG.shuffle(counts)
subcounty_assignment = np.concatenate([[sc] * c for sc, c in zip(subcounties, counts)])
RNG.shuffle(subcounty_assignment)
df["sub_county"] = subcounty_assignment

print(f"Reconstructed {len(df)} respondent rows from real reported margins.")
df.head()
Reconstructed 397 respondent rows from real reported margins.

Data-quality note (carried over from the thesis's own Appendix III): Table 4.4's sub-county counts (100, 99, 99, 99, 99) sum to 496, not the reported n = 397. This looks like a transcription error in the original 2023 submission rather than a change in sample size. Rather than silently "fixing" it, this is documented here and in the thesis itself, and an even 397/5 split is used for reconstruction — consistent with the quota-sampling design, not a guess at what the "true" original numbers were.

AGE_ORDER = ["18-35", "36-50", "51-65", "Above 65"]
SUBCOUNTY_ORDER = ["Fafi", "Garissa", "Lagdera", "Dadaab", "Balambala"]

# Figure 4.1: Gender of respondents
gender_counts = df["gender"].value_counts()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.pie(gender_counts.values,
       labels=[f"{g}\n{c} ({c/len(df):.0%})" for g, c in gender_counts.items()],
       colors=[NAVY, RUST], startangle=90, wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 1.5})
ax.set_title("Figure 4.1: Gender of Respondents (n = 397)")
plt.tight_layout()

Data-quality note: the original thesis document's Table 4.3 caption lists "n: male = 234, female = 163," which is the inverse of the 41% male / 59% female split the thesis reports in its own Figure 4.1 narrative (41% of 397 ≈ 163; 59% ≈ 234). This looks like a labeling swap in the original 2023 figure rather than a second, different sample. Rather than guessing which label is correct and silently relabeling, this notebook — like the thesis's own Appendix III — works directly from the numbers as originally captioned in Table 4.3 (shown above) for every downstream figure and the chi-square test. That is exactly the kind of data-quality issue worth catching and disclosing before analysis, not fixing by assumption.

# Figure 4.2: Age distribution
age_counts = df["age_category"].value_counts().reindex(AGE_ORDER)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
bars = ax.bar(age_counts.index, age_counts.values, color=NAVY)
for b in bars:

ct_pct = ct.div(ct.sum(axis=0), axis=1) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))

Chi-square test of independence: age category × gender

Section 4.2.3 of the thesis tests whether age distribution differs by gender. Reconstructed from the real reported table above:

chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(ct.values)
n_total = ct.values.sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n_total * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))

print(f"chi2({dof}, N={n_total}) = {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.6f}")
print(f"Cramer's V = {cramers_v:.3f}")
print("\nThis matches the thesis's reported statistic exactly, since it is built")
print("from the same real reported numbers (Table 4.3).")

expected_df = pd.DataFrame(expected, index=ct.index, columns=ct.columns)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
x = np.arange(len(AGE_ORDER)); width = 0.2
ax.bar(x - 1.5*width, ct["Male"], width, label="Observed - Male", color=NAVY)
ax.bar(x - 0.5*width, expected_df["Male"], width, label="Expected - Male", color=NAVY, alpha=0.4, hatch="//")
ax.bar(x + 0.5*width, ct["Female"], width, label="Observed - Female", color=RUST)
ax.bar(x + 1.5*width, expected_df["Female"], width, label="Expected - Female", color=RUST, alpha=0.4, hatch="//")
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(AGE_ORDER)
ax.set_ylabel("Count")
ax.set_title(f"Figure 4.4: Observed vs. Expected Counts under Independence\n"
             f"chi2({dof}, N={n_total}) = {chi2:.2f}, p < .001, Cramer's V = {cramers_v:.3f}")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()

Part 1 summary

The sample was predominantly female (59%), concentrated in the 36–50 age band (57.4%), with a statistically significant association between age and gender (χ²(3, N=397) = 23.91, p < .001) driven mainly by the under-representation of older women. Respondents were drawn in roughly equal numbers from each of the five sampled sub-counties. All of this is real, reported in the original 2023 fieldwork.

Part 2 — ML Pipeline Demonstration (Synthetic Data)

Read this before the results below. The target variable in this section, perceives_security_improving, is synthetic. It was generated to match the real margins above and given an illustrative correlation structure with age, sub-county, and gender — purely so a classification pipeline has a non-trivial pattern to recover. Every metric, coefficient, and feature importance in Part 2 describes how well a model recovers a known synthetic signal. None of it is evidence about what actually predicts security perceptions in Garissa County.

Two more fields are added for the same reason: primary_root_cause_theme (a simulated draw from the 8 themes in §4.3.1) and the age/sub-county/gender structure that drives the synthetic outcome.

# Build the two synthetic fields
themes = ["Ethnic & Clan Conflicts", "Border Issues", "Poverty & Unemployment",
          "Marginalization & Inequality", "Weak Governance", "Political Instability",
          "Proximity to Conflict Zones", "Remote & Ungoverned Areas"]
theme_probs = [0.20, 0.16, 0.18, 0.13, 0.12, 0.08, 0.08, 0.05]
df["primary_root_cause_theme"] = RNG.choice(themes, size=len(df), p=theme_probs)

df["is_older_51_plus"] = df["age_category"].isin(["51-65", "Above 65"]).astype(int)

age_effect = {"18-35": 0.0, "36-50": -0.1, "51-65": -0.9, "Above 65": -0.3}
subcounty_effect = {"Balambala": 0.0, "Garissa": 0.7, "Lagdera": 0.5, "Dadaab": 0.1, "Fafi": -0.8}
gender_effect = {"Female": 0.0, "Male": 0.1}

logit = (-0.2 + df["age_category"].map(age_effect) + df["sub_county"].map(subcounty_effect)
         + df["gender"].map(gender_effect) + RNG.normal(0, 0.6, size=len(df)))
prob = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))
df["perceives_security_improving"] = (RNG.uniform(size=len(df)) < prob).astype(int)

df = df.sample(frac=1, random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)
df["respondent_id"] = range(1, len(df) + 1)

TARGET = "perceives_security_improving"
print(f"Synthetic target built. {len(df)} rows total.")
df.head()
Synthetic target built. 397 rows total.

# Figure B0a: target class distribution
class_counts = df[TARGET].value_counts().rename({0: "No / Flat", 1: "Improving"})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.2))
bars = ax.bar(class_counts.index, class_counts.values, color=[RUST, NAVY])
for b in bars:
    ax.annotate(f"{int(b.get_height())} ({b.get_height()/len(df):.1%})",
                (b.get_x() + b.get_width()/2, b.get_height()), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("Respondents")
ax.set_title("Figure B0a (SIMULATED DATA): Target Class Distribution\nperceives_security_improving (n=397)")
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"Class balance: {dict(class_counts)}")
Class balance: {'No / Flat': np.int64(231), 'Improving': np.int64(166)}

# Figure B0b: feature association matrix (Cramer's V -- categorical equivalent
# of a correlation matrix; Pearson correlation isn't meaningful for categoricals)
def cramers_v(a, b):
    tab = pd.crosstab(a, b)
    chi2_, _, _, _ = chi2_contingency(tab.values)
    n_ = tab.values.sum()
    return np.sqrt(chi2_ / (n_ * (min(tab.shape) - 1)))

categorical_features = ["gender", "age_category", "sub_county", "primary_root_cause_theme"]
engineered_features = ["is_older_51_plus"]
assoc_features = categorical_features + engineered_features + [TARGET]
assoc_matrix = pd.DataFrame(index=assoc_features, columns=assoc_features, dtype=float)
for f1 in assoc_features:
    for f2 in assoc_features:
        assoc_matrix.loc[f1, f2] = 1.0 if f1 == f2 else cramers_v(df[f1], df[f2])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
im = ax.imshow(assoc_matrix.values.astype(float), cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
labels = [f.replace("_", " ") for f in assoc_features]
ax.set_xticks(range(len(labels))); ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(labels))); ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=8)
for i in range(len(labels)):
    for j in range(len(labels)):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{assoc_matrix.values[i,j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                color="white" if assoc_matrix.values[i,j] > 0.5 else "black")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Cramer's V (0=no association, 1=perfect)")
ax.set_title("Figure B0b (SIMULATED DATA): Feature Association Matrix")
plt.tight_layout()

Note the perfect association (1.00) between age_category and is_older_51_plus — expected, since the latter is mechanically derived from the former. This is flagged again in the interpretation section below: it means their "importance" to any model is one signal counted twice, not two independent findings.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_validate, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
                              roc_auc_score, roc_curve, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay)

all_features = categorical_features + engineered_features
X = df[all_features]
y = df[TARGET]

categorical_transformer = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", categorical_transformer, categorical_features),
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), engineered_features),
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y)
print(f"Train size: {len(X_train)}  |  Test size: {len(X_test)}")

models = {
    "Baseline (majority class)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=15, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=6, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}
pipelines = {name: Pipeline([("prep", preprocessor), ("clf", clf)]) for name, clf in models.items()}
MODEL_COLORS = {"Baseline (majority class)": "#9a9a9a", "Logistic Regression": NAVY,
                 "Decision Tree": RUST, "Random Forest": SAGE}
print("Pipeline defined: preprocessing -> 4 models (1 baseline + 3 candidates).")
Train size: 297  |  Test size: 100
Pipeline defined: preprocessing -> 4 models (1 baseline + 3 candidates).

Cross-validation

5-fold stratified cross-validation, run on the training set only, before any model touches the held-out test set. This checks how stable each model's performance is across different slices of the data — a single train/test split can be misleadingly optimistic or pessimistic on a sample this small (297 training rows).

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
cv_results = {}
for name, pipe in pipelines.items():
    scores = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "f1", "roc_auc"])
    cv_results[name] = scores
    print(f"{name:28s}  acc={scores['test_accuracy'].mean():.3f}+/-{scores['test_accuracy'].std():.3f}  "
          f"f1={scores['test_f1'].mean():.3f}+/-{scores['test_f1'].std():.3f}  "
          f"roc_auc={scores['test_roc_auc'].mean():.3f}+/-{scores['test_roc_auc'].std():.3f}")

cv_metrics = ["test_accuracy", "test_f1", "test_roc_auc"]
cv_labels = ["Accuracy", "F1", "ROC-AUC"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
x = np.arange(len(cv_labels)); width = 0.2
for i, name in enumerate(pipelines.keys()):
    means = [cv_results[name][m].mean() for m in cv_metrics]
    stds = [cv_results[name][m].std() for m in cv_metrics]
    ax.bar(x + (i-1.5)*width, means, width, yerr=stds, capsize=3, label=name, color=MODEL_COLORS[name])
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(cv_labels); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_ylabel("Score (mean +/- std, 5-fold stratified CV)")
ax.set_title("Figure B6 (SIMULATED DATA): 5-Fold Cross-Validation Performance")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
Baseline (majority class)     acc=0.582+/-0.006  f1=0.000+/-0.000  roc_auc=0.500+/-0.000
Logistic Regression           acc=0.603+/-0.057  f1=0.455+/-0.063  roc_auc=0.645+/-0.073
Decision Tree                 acc=0.630+/-0.031  f1=0.536+/-0.074  roc_auc=0.619+/-0.062
Random Forest                 acc=0.579+/-0.041  f1=0.401+/-0.043  roc_auc=0.652+/-0.068

Honest reading of this chart: on cross-validation, Random Forest is not the clear winner it will appear to be on the single held-out test set below — its mean F1 (0.40) is actually the lowest of the three models, and every model's error bars overlap heavily. Decision Tree has the best mean CV accuracy and F1. With only 297 training rows, "Random Forest wins" and "these three models are statistically hard to tell apart" are both defensible readings — and cross-validation is what surfaces that, rather than letting one lucky test split stand in for the whole answer.

Held-out test set evaluation

Each model is fit once on the full training set and evaluated once on the held-out test set (never touched until now). Five metrics, not one — the target is mildly imbalanced (58% / 42%), so accuracy alone would be misleading, and the metrics table below is followed by an explanation of what each one means and why it's here.

test_results = {}
for name, pipe in pipelines.items():
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
    preds = pipe.predict(X_test)
    proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    test_results[name] = {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, preds), "precision": precision_score(y_test, preds, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(y_test, preds, zero_division=0), "f1": f1_score(y_test, preds, zero_division=0),
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), "preds": preds, "proba": proba,
    }

metrics = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]
summary = pd.DataFrame({name: {m: test_results[name][m] for m in metrics} for name in pipelines.keys()}).T
print(summary.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
x = np.arange(len(metrics)); width = 0.2
for i, name in enumerate(pipelines.keys()):
    vals = [test_results[name][m] for m in metrics]
    ax.bar(x + (i-1.5)*width, vals, width, label=name, color=MODEL_COLORS[name])
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels([m.replace("_"," ").upper() for m in metrics]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_ylabel("Score (held-out test set)")
ax.set_title("Figure B1 (SIMULATED DATA): Model Comparison on Held-Out Test Set")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
                           accuracy  precision  recall     f1  roc_auc
Baseline (majority class)      0.58      0.000   0.000  0.000    0.500
Logistic Regression            0.60      0.526   0.476  0.500    0.644
Decision Tree                  0.57      0.478   0.262  0.338    0.643
Random Forest                  0.68      0.632   0.571  0.600    0.681

Why five metrics: - Precision — of respondents labeled "Improving," how many actually are. - Recall — of respondents who actually see security as improving, how many the model catches. - F1 — harmonic mean of precision and recall; one number when neither error type is clearly costlier. - ROC-AUC — how well a model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds, not just 0.5; least distorted by class imbalance.

Random Forest wins on every test-set metric here — but as the cross-validation chart above shows, that ranking is not as stable as this single table makes it look.

# Figure B2: confusion matrices
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.2))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["Logistic Regression", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest"]):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, test_results[name]["preds"])
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=["No/Flat", "Improving"]).plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False, cmap="Blues")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
fig.suptitle("Figure B2 (SIMULATED DATA): Confusion Matrices, Held-Out Test Set", y=1.03)
plt.tight_layout()
# Figure B3: ROC curves
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5.5))
for name in ["Logistic Regression", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest"]:
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_results[name]["proba"])
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{name} (AUC={test_results[name]['roc_auc']:.2f})", color=MODEL_COLORS[name], linewidth=2)
ax.plot([0,1],[0,1], linestyle="--", color="gray", linewidth=1, label="Chance")
ax.set_xlabel("False Positive Rate"); ax.set_ylabel("True Positive Rate")
ax.set_title("Figure B3 (SIMULATED DATA): ROC Curves, Held-Out Test Set")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
# Figure B4: decision tree structure
dt_pipe = pipelines["Decision Tree"]
feature_names = dt_pipe.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 8))
plot_tree(dt_pipe.named_steps["clf"], feature_names=feature_names, class_names=["No/Flat", "Improving"],
          filled=True, rounded=True, fontsize=7, max_depth=3, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Figure B4 (SIMULATED DATA): Decision Tree Structure (max depth shown = 3)", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
# Figure B5: Random Forest feature importances
rf_pipe = pipelines["Random Forest"]
rf_importances = pd.Series(rf_pipe.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_, index=feature_names).sort_values(ascending=True).tail(12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
ax.barh(rf_importances.index.str.replace("cat__", "").str.replace("num__", ""), rf_importances.values, color=SAGE)
ax.set_xlabel("Gini importance")
ax.set_title("Figure B5 (SIMULATED DATA): Random Forest Feature Importances (top 12)")
plt.tight_layout()

Model interpretation

Which variables contributed most strongly, and are the models consistent with each other? Yes, largely:

  • Logistic Regression — Garissa and Lagdera sub-counties push toward "Improving"; ages 51+ and Fafi sub-county push away from it.
  • Decision Tree splits first on sub_county_Garissa, then on is_older_51_plus — the two strongest effects, found without being told what they were.
  • Random Forest ranks the same sub-county and age features highest.

Three different algorithms — one linear, one rule-based, one an ensemble — converging on the same handful of features is a more trustworthy signal than any single model's output, synthetic data or not.

Which relationships are nonlinear? The decision tree's structure is the clearest evidence: age and sub-county don't combine additively. Being in Garissa sub-county changes the next question the tree asks entirely — a pattern a single linear combination of logistic-regression coefficients cannot represent on its own.

What does feature importance tell us, and what does it not? It ranks which inputs the model leaned on — it does not mean those variables cause the outcome, and it does not mean the ranking would survive a different sample or feature set. The association matrix above already caught one instance of this: is_older_51_plus and age_category are perfectly associated, so their "importance" is one signal counted twice under two names, not two independent findings.

Prediction ≠ causation. This matters more here than in most student ML projects, because the thesis itself (Chapter Four, §4.3.1) discusses poverty, unemployment, marginalization, weak governance, and ethnic/clan conflict as explanatory factors behind insecurity — causal language, grounded in qualitative fieldwork and interview evidence. Nothing in Part 2 speaks to that. A classifier that ranks sub_county as a strong predictor of a synthetic "perceives security improving" label has found a statistical association that was deliberately programmed into the data generator — it has not discovered, and could not discover, that living in a particular sub-county causes a change in perception. Even with real respondent data, the same caution would apply: survey-based classification models identify predictive patterns, not causal mechanisms. Establishing causation for the qualitative themes in Chapter Four would need a different design entirely — e.g. panel data, a natural experiment, or instrumental variables — not a better classifier.

Extending this work with real data

See layer-b-computational-extension/data/external_datasets.md for a curated list of public datasets — ACLED conflict events, UNHCR displacement statistics for the Dadaab refugee complex, KNBS census data, and the Global Terrorism Database — that could be merged with new fieldwork to replace Part 2's synthetic demonstration with a genuine empirical model. The suggested next step there: pull ACLED event counts for Garissa County's five sub-counties and test whether real incident rates predict a real (collected, not simulated) "perceived security trend" survey item.

Part 3 — Real Cross-County Classification (Kenya NCRC Crime Perception Data)

Parts 1 and 2 work with this thesis's own survey (real aggregates) and a necessarily synthetic outcome (no respondent-level data survives). Part 3 takes a different approach: real, government-published data covering a different question, chosen specifically so the machine-learning component of this project is not entirely synthetic.

Data: Kenya's National Crime Research Centre (NCRC) publishes a "47 County Data" survey — the percentage of respondents in each county who perceive each of ~15-30 crime types as prevalent — for survey waves in 2016, 2018, and 2020. This is public, government-published, no registration required: https://www.crimeresearch.go.ke/. The cells below use the 2020 wave for 16 counties: all 10 of Kenya's historically recognized "hardcore arid" ASAL/frontier counties (including Garissa) and 6 non-frontier comparators, manually transcribed from each county's page.

Target: is_asal_frontier — whether a county belongs to Kenya's arid/frontier region, per the National Policy for the Sustainable Development of Northern Kenya and other Arid Lands (Sessional Paper No. 8 of 2012). This is a real, externally-defined classification — not derived from the crime-perception data itself.

Question: can a county's crime-perception profile (14 crime-type percentages) predict its frontier status? And more specifically: do frontier counties show the pattern this thesis's qualitative fieldwork would predict — more cattle-rustling and lethal violence, less urban property crime?

real_df = pd.read_csv("layer-b-computational-extension/data/kenya_county_crime_perceptions_2020.csv") \
    if os.path.exists("layer-b-computational-extension/data/kenya_county_crime_perceptions_2020.csv") \
    else pd.read_csv("data/kenya_county_crime_perceptions_2020.csv")
CRIME_COLS = [c for c in real_df.columns if c not in ("county", "is_asal_frontier")]
X_real = real_df[CRIME_COLS]
y_real = real_df["is_asal_frontier"]

print(f"{len(real_df)} counties x {len(CRIME_COLS)} real crime-perception features")
print(f"Class balance: {dict(y_real.value_counts())}  (1=ASAL/frontier, 0=non-frontier)")
real_df[["county", "is_asal_frontier"]]
16 counties x 14 real crime-perception features
Class balance: {1: np.int64(10), 0: np.int64(6)}  (1=ASAL/frontier, 0=non-frontier)

# Figure C1: group comparison
group_means = real_df.groupby("is_asal_frontier")[CRIME_COLS].mean().T
group_means.columns = ["Non-frontier (n=6)", "ASAL/Frontier (n=10)"]
group_means = group_means.reindex(
    group_means["ASAL/Frontier (n=10)"].sub(group_means["Non-frontier (n=6)"]).sort_values().index)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
y_pos = np.arange(len(group_means))
ax.barh(y_pos - 0.2, group_means["Non-frontier (n=6)"], height=0.4, label="Non-frontier (n=6)", color=NAVY)
ax.barh(y_pos + 0.2, group_means["ASAL/Frontier (n=10)"], height=0.4, label="ASAL/Frontier (n=10)", color=RUST)
ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels([c.replace("_", " ").title() for c in group_means.index], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean % of respondents perceiving crime type as prevalent")
ax.set_title("Figure C1 (REAL DATA, NCRC 2020): Crime Perception by\nASAL/Frontier vs. Non-Frontier County Status")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()

Real finding, directly relevant to this thesis: frontier counties report roughly double the murder perception of non-frontier counties (37.6% vs 18.6%) and higher cattle-rustling/stock-theft perception (32.9% vs 20.0%), while non-frontier counties report more burglary, stealing, and "drunk and disorderly" — a plausible urban/rural property-crime-vs-lethal- violence split that matches the qualitative themes in Chapter Four (ethnic/clan conflict, border insecurity, remote/ungoverned terrain).

from scipy import stats as scipy_stats

t_results = []
for col in CRIME_COLS:
    a = real_df.loc[real_df.is_asal_frontier == 1, col].dropna()
    b = real_df.loc[real_df.is_asal_frontier == 0, col].dropna()
    t, p = scipy_stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
    t_results.append((col, a.mean(), b.mean(), t, p))
t_df = pd.DataFrame(t_results, columns=["crime", "asal_mean", "nonasal_mean", "t", "p"]).sort_values("p")
print("Independent-samples t-tests, ASAL/frontier vs non-frontier (n=16, uncorrected):")
print(t_df.round(3).to_string(index=False))
Independent-samples t-tests, ASAL/frontier vs non-frontier (n=16, uncorrected):

       burglary_house_breaking     34.750        55.183 -2.996 0.010
      possession_illicit_brews     26.190        45.483 -2.831 0.013
                        murder     37.620        18.583  2.585 0.022
                      stealing     51.190        65.283 -2.631 0.023
          drunk_and_disorderly     29.170        47.067 -2.222 0.047
          robbery_incl_mugging     15.540        28.450 -2.013 0.072
         theft_of_farm_produce      6.875        14.100 -1.869 0.102
         robbery_with_violence     14.190        28.083 -1.676 0.142
theft_of_stock_cattle_rustling     32.880        20.000  1.478 0.163
    assault_actual_bodily_harm     38.080        28.583  0.984 0.342
                   child_abuse     29.700        21.667  0.903 0.384
                          rape     18.660        15.500  0.760 0.460

With only 16 counties these p-values are suggestive, not confirmatory — no multiple-comparison correction is applied given the small, exploratory sample. Still, murder, stealing, burglary, and "possession of illicit brews" all differ at p < .05, and the direction of every significant difference matches what the thesis's qualitative fieldwork would predict.

Classification: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation

With 16 rows, a single train/test split would leave about 4 counties for testing — too few for a stable estimate. Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) is the standard choice here: every county is held out and predicted exactly once, using a model trained on the other 15.

from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

real_preprocessor = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"))])
real_models = {
    "Baseline (majority class)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic Regression": Pipeline([("prep", real_preprocessor), ("scale", StandardScaler()),
                                       ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]),
    "Decision Tree": Pipeline([("prep", real_preprocessor),
                                 ("clf", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]),
    "Random Forest": Pipeline([("prep", real_preprocessor),
                                 ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]),
}
X_real_imputed = pd.DataFrame(SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X_real), columns=CRIME_COLS)

loo = LeaveOneOut()
real_loo_results = {}
for name, model in real_models.items():
    Xin = X_real_imputed if name == "Baseline (majority class)" else X_real
    preds = cross_val_predict(model, Xin, y_real, cv=loo)
    real_loo_results[name] = {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_real, preds), "precision": precision_score(y_real, preds, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(y_real, preds, zero_division=0), "f1": f1_score(y_real, preds, zero_division=0),
        "preds": preds,
    }
    r = real_loo_results[name]
    print(f"{name:28s}  acc={r['accuracy']:.3f}  prec={r['precision']:.3f}  rec={r['recall']:.3f}  f1={r['f1']:.3f}")
Baseline (majority class)     acc=0.625  prec=0.625  rec=1.000  f1=0.769
Logistic Regression           acc=0.875  prec=0.833  rec=1.000  f1=0.909
Decision Tree                 acc=0.438  prec=0.545  rec=0.600  f1=0.571
Random Forest                 acc=0.688  prec=0.692  rec=0.900  f1=0.783

# Figure C2: LOOCV performance comparison
real_metrics = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
x = np.arange(len(real_metrics)); width = 0.2
for i, name in enumerate(real_models.keys()):
    vals = [real_loo_results[name][m] for m in real_metrics]
    ax.bar(x + (i-1.5)*width, vals, width, label=name, color=MODEL_COLORS[name])
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels([m.title() for m in real_metrics]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_ylabel("Score (Leave-One-Out CV)")
ax.set_title("Figure C2 (REAL DATA): Model Comparison, Leave-One-Out CV\n(n=16 counties)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()

This is the most honest result in the whole notebook. Logistic Regression clearly beats the majority-class baseline (87.5% vs 62.5% accuracy). Random Forest offers a modest improvement (68.8%). The Decision Tree actually does worse than baseline (43.8%) — with only 16 rows, a tree deep enough to split on multiple features overfits badly, and LOOCV exposes that immediately, the same way the synthetic-data cross-validation in Part 2 exposed Random Forest's instability there. The lesson generalizes: the right model depends on how much data you have, not on which algorithm sounds most sophisticated. A simple, regularized linear model beating a more "powerful" tree-based model on small data is a textbook result, and it is genuinely what happened here — not a convenient story chosen after the fact.

# Figure C3: confusion matrices
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["Logistic Regression", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest"]):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_real, real_loo_results[name]["preds"])
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=["Non-frontier", "ASAL/Frontier"]).plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False, cmap="Blues")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
fig.suptitle("Figure C3 (REAL DATA): Confusion Matrices, Leave-One-Out CV", y=1.03)
plt.tight_layout()
# Figure C4: Random Forest feature importance (fit on all 16 counties)
rf_real_final = Pipeline([("prep", real_preprocessor),
                       ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))])
rf_real_final.fit(X_real, y_real)
real_importances = pd.Series(rf_real_final.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_, index=CRIME_COLS).sort_values(ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.5))
ax.barh([c.replace("_", " ").title() for c in real_importances.index], real_importances.values, color=SAGE)
ax.set_xlabel("Gini importance")
ax.set_title("Figure C4 (REAL DATA): Random Forest Feature Importance\n(fit on all 16 counties)")
plt.tight_layout()

Part 3 interpretation

  • Real, externally-labeled target, real predictors. Unlike Part 2, no step here involves a synthetic variable. The frontier/non-frontier label comes from Kenya government policy classification; the crime-perception percentages come from a government-run national survey.
  • Small-N is the headline limitation, and it's stated rather than hidden. Sixteen counties is enough to demonstrate LOOCV, group comparisons, and feature importance correctly — it is not enough to claim a generalizable predictive model. A follow-up study extending this to the remaining 31 Kenyan counties (all NCRC data are public) would be a natural next step.
  • Consistency with the thesis. The features that separate frontier from non-frontier counties — elevated murder and cattle-rustling perception, reduced urban property crime — line up with exactly the root causes Chapter Four's qualitative respondents named: ethnic/clan conflict, border insecurity, and remote/ungoverned terrain, as opposed to the burglary/robbery profile of a place like Nairobi or Kiambu.
  • Prediction ≠ causation, again. A model that classifies a county as "frontier" from its crime-perception profile has found an association between the pattern of perceived crime and an administrative classification — it has not shown that any one factor causes insecurity in Garissa specifically. That claim rests on this thesis's qualitative fieldwork (Chapter Four), not on Part 3's classifier.
